units.subject: English Language
units.title: Sounds around us
units.objective: Recognise and name common sound sources.
explanation: People, animals and objects make different sounds. Birds chirp, dogs bark and bells ring. Listen carefully before identifying what made a sound.
Ask a trusted adult to clap hands, shake a bell or tap a table softly. Name each sound source and tell how the sounds differ.
units.workedExample: When we hear a bell ring, the bell is the source of the sound.
units.question: Which object can ring?
units.feedback: A bell makes a ringing sound.

exercises.question: Name two animal sounds.
exercises.answer: For example: dog barks; bird chirps.

assignment.title: Sounds around us — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Listen for three safe sounds around home or school. Draw each source and explain it to a teacher.

units.mediaActivity: Teacher demonstration of sounds; use new illustrations rather than copied workbook pictures.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Greetings and polite replies
units.objective: Use a suitable greeting at different times of day.
explanation: Greetings begin friendly conversations. Say 'Good morning' early in the day and 'Good afternoon' later. Listen respectfully to the reply.
Practise greeting a teacher, a friend and a family member. Learners may use signing or home-language greetings as appropriate.
units.workedExample: Good morning, Teacher. Good morning, how are you? I am well, thank you.
units.question: Which greeting is suitable before lessons begin?
units.feedback: Good morning is suitable at the beginning of the day.

assignment.title: Greetings and polite replies — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Act out two everyday greetings with a partner. Show careful listening and polite replies.

units.mediaActivity: Consent-based learner role-play; no real addresses or phone numbers.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Sequencing picture stories
units.objective: Arrange a story into first, next and last.
explanation: Stories have events that take place in a sequence. We can understand the order by looking closely at pictures before we read full sentences.
Imagine three pictures showing a child planting a seed, watering it and seeing it sprout. Tell what happened first, next and last.
units.workedExample: First Chipo plants a seed. Next she waters it. Last a shoot grows.
units.question: What must happen before watering a newly planted seed?
units.feedback: Planting the seed is the first step.

assignment.title: Sequencing picture stories — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw three original pictures showing a simple sequence and describe the order aloud.

units.mediaActivity: Learner-created three-panel story.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Tracing patterns and the letter O
units.objective: Practise lines, curves and early letter shapes.
explanation: Early writing begins with moving a pencil carefully across the page. Straight strokes, loops and circles develop control and hand-eye coordination.
Trace a large round shape, then try forming the capital letter O. Use safe pencil grip, take breaks and use tactile shapes where needed.
units.workedExample: A capital O is one smooth closed round line.
units.question: Which shape best helps you practise O?
units.feedback: O is formed from a rounded closed curve.

assignment.title: Tracing patterns and the letter O — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Create three rows of traced patterns and one row showing the first letter of your name.

units.mediaActivity: Original large-print tracing card or tactile equivalent.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Washing hands with soap
units.objective: Show appropriate handwashing actions.
explanation: Hands pick up dirt and germs when we play and touch surfaces. Washing with clean water and soap helps remove unwanted material.
Wet hands, apply soap, rub palms and backs of hands, clean between fingers, rinse and dry hygienically. Wash before eating and after using the toilet.
units.workedExample: Tariro washes her hands after playing outside and before eating lunch.
units.question: When should we wash our hands?
units.feedback: Washing before eating helps keep us healthy.

exercises.question: When should we wash after using a toilet?

assignment.title: Washing hands with soap — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Demonstrate handwashing and draw two times when it is important.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Infant Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Live demonstration with safe water and soap.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Foods from plants and animals
units.objective: Sort foods according to their sources.
explanation: Maize, groundnuts, vegetables and fruit grow on plants. Eggs and milk are examples of foods that come from animals.
Use real safe foods or pictures to make two groups. Ask where each food originates rather than guessing from its packaging.
units.workedExample: Maize comes from a plant. Milk may come from a cow or goat.
units.question: Which comes from a plant?
units.feedback: Maize is grown and harvested from plants.

exercises.question: Name two plant foods.
exercises.answer: Maize and vegetables, or other correct examples.

assignment.title: Foods from plants and animals — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw four foods available locally, then group them by plant or animal source.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Infant Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Real foods or fresh learner drawings.

units.subject: Indigenous Languages
units.title: Greetings and Unhu
units.objective: Show respect through culturally suitable greetings.
explanation: Zimbabwean communities use a range of indigenous languages and greeting traditions. Respect includes waiting for a response and using polite words.
In Shona, 'Mangwanani' can be used as a morning greeting. Invite learners to share other locally appropriate expressions without treating one language as universal.
units.workedExample: A child greets an older person politely, listens and answers the greeting.
units.question: What best shows respect while greeting?
units.feedback: Unhu includes listening and responding respectfully.

exercises.question: Give a greeting in a familiar local language.

assignment.title: Greetings and Unhu — class assignment
assignment.instructions: With consent, ask a family member to teach two greetings and demonstrate where each is appropriate.

units.mediaActivity: Optional live greeting demonstration; do not collect private contact details.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Following two instructions
units.objective: Perform two safe actions in the correct order.
explanation: When someone gives two instructions, listen to both before you begin. Remember which action comes first and which follows it.
Try 'point to the window, then clap once'. Complete the first instruction before doing the second.
units.workedExample: Close the book and put it on the desk: close it first; place it on the desk second.
units.question: Which action comes first when told 'stand up, then sit down'?
units.feedback: Standing up comes before sitting down.

assignment.title: Following two instructions — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Invent two short classroom instructions for a partner and check that the order is followed.

units.mediaActivity: Teacher-recorded voice instruction or signing demonstration.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Recording the weather
units.objective: Name common weather conditions and record observations.
explanation: Weather may be sunny, cloudy, windy or rainy. Observing conditions helps us choose suitable clothing and plan everyday activities.
Make a small three-day chart and describe conditions while staying safe. Do not go outside to observe lightning or violent storms.
units.workedExample: A rainy morning may be recorded as cloudy and wet. A raincoat can help a learner stay dry.
units.question: What clothing helps in rain?
units.feedback: A raincoat is useful during rainy weather.

exercises.question: What is safe during lightning?
exercises.answer: Remain in a suitable shelter with adult guidance.

assignment.title: Recording the weather — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Keep a three-day weather chart using words or pictures and explain one suitable clothing choice.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Infant Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Student-made weather symbols and chart.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Place value up to one thousand
units.objective: Identify hundreds, tens and units.
explanation: In the number 472, the 4 represents four hundreds, the 7 represents seven tens and the 2 represents two units.
We can write 472 as 400 + 70 + 2. Use bundles of sticks or a place-value chart to check each digit.
units.workedExample: 305 = 300 + 0 tens + 5 units.
units.question: What is the value of 6 in 648?
units.feedback: 6 is in the hundreds place and is worth 600.

exercises.question: What is the tens digit in 719?
Write four hundreds and six units.

assignment.title: Place value up to one thousand — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Create a place-value table for 736 and explain the value of each digit.

units.mediaActivity: Homemade counters and hundreds-tens-units chart.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Multiplication as equal groups
units.objective: Calculate products using repeated addition.
explanation: Equal groups have the same number of items. Three groups of four counters contain 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 counters.
Multiplication is a short way to describe equal groups. Three groups of four are written 3 × 4 = 12.
units.workedExample: Four plates with two bananas each show 4 × 2 = 8.
units.question: What is 3 × 5?
units.feedback: Three equal groups of five make fifteen.

exercises.question: Draw two groups of six.
exercises.answer: Twelve counters arranged in two groups.

assignment.title: Multiplication as equal groups — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw three examples of equal groups from home or school and work out their totals.

units.mediaActivity: Stones or bottle tops for groups.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Main idea and supporting detail
units.objective: Identify what an original story is mostly about.
explanation: Read: 'Rudo planted a small garden. She watered it each morning. Green shoots appeared after several days.'
The main idea is that Rudo grew and cared for plants. The details tell what she did and what happened afterward.
units.workedExample: Main idea: Rudo cared for her garden. Detail: she watered it in the morning.
units.question: What is the story mainly about?
units.feedback: Every sentence relates to Rudo's small garden.

exercises.question: Write the main idea.
exercises.answer: Rudo grew plants in a garden.

assignment.title: Main idea and supporting detail — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Read a new short classroom story and give its main idea plus two details.

units.mediaActivity: Learner-created picture of a garden.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Food sources and good hygiene
units.objective: Classify common foods and explain basic handling.
explanation: Foods such as maize, groundnuts and vegetables come from plants. Other foods such as eggs and milk are produced by animals.
Food sources can be identified by asking how each item is grown or produced. Clean preparation and safe storage help reduce contamination.
units.workedExample: An egg is an animal-derived food; a mango is a plant-derived food.
units.question: Which food comes from an animal?
units.feedback: Eggs are produced by birds such as chickens.

exercises.question: Give one food-hygiene step.
exercises.answer: Wash hands and use clean utensils.

assignment.title: Food sources and good hygiene — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Make a two-column table of six local foods, classify them by source and explain safe handling for one.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Original food-source pictures or safe food samples.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Common nouns and proper nouns
units.objective: Identify nouns and use capital letters in proper names.
explanation: Nouns name people, places, animals and things. Words such as 'school', 'goat' and 'teacher' are common nouns.
Proper nouns identify particular people and places. Names such as Zimbabwe, Harare and Tariro begin with capital letters.
units.workedExample: Tariro visited Kwekwe. Tariro and Kwekwe are proper nouns.
units.question: Which word is a proper noun?
units.feedback: Zimbabwe names a particular country.

exercises.question: Find nouns in 'A goat eats grass'.

assignment.title: Common nouns and proper nouns — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Write six original sentences containing at least three common nouns and three proper nouns.

units.mediaActivity: Teacher-authored sentences; avoid copying commercial passages.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: A friendly letter
units.objective: Write an informal letter with a greeting, body and closing.
explanation: A friendly letter shares news and experiences with someone you know. Begin with an appropriate greeting and communicate in clear sentences.
Organise ideas into short paragraphs and use a suitable closing. Proofread spelling, punctuation and capital letters before sharing.
units.workedExample: Dear Auntie, Our class planted vegetables today. I hope to see you soon. Yours lovingly, Nyasha.
units.question: Which opening fits a friendly letter?
units.feedback: Dear Grandma is personal and polite.

exercises.question: Write an opening to a friend.

assignment.title: A friendly letter — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Write 100–150 words to a relative about a school activity; do not include a real private address.

units.mediaActivity: Original handwriting template or safe typed format.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Four-digit place value
units.objective: Read and expand numbers up to ten thousand.
explanation: Each position in a four-digit number has a value. In 6,204, the digit 6 stands for six thousands and 2 stands for two hundreds.
Expanded notation shows the values separately. We can write 6,204 as 6,000 + 200 + 4.
units.workedExample: In 8,530 there are 8 thousands, 5 hundreds, 3 tens and 0 units.
units.question: What is the value of 7 in 7,412?
units.feedback: The 7 is in the thousands position.

assignment.title: Four-digit place value — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Record five four-digit numbers on a place-value chart and order them from smallest to largest.

units.mediaActivity: Cardboard number cards and place-value pockets.

units.subject: Indigenous Languages
units.title: Retelling a folktale
units.objective: Retell story events and explain a moral.
explanation: Folktales are stories passed on in families and communities. Their characters may include people or talking animals.
Listen to a folktale in a familiar indigenous language. Retell its beginning, middle and end and explain the lesson it teaches.
units.workedExample: A hare refuses to help neighbours, then needs their help. This story can teach cooperation.
units.question: What shows understanding of a folktale?
units.feedback: Retelling and discussing the moral demonstrates comprehension.

exercises.question: Name one part of a story.
What is a moral?
exercises.answer: The lesson learned from a story.

assignment.title: Retelling a folktale — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Listen to a permitted local folktale and retell it in your own words, including its message.

units.mediaActivity: Consent-based family storytelling; no reproduction of publisher art.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: The digestive system
units.objective: Identify main digestive organs and their roles.
explanation: Food passes through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach and intestines. Chewing breaks food into small pieces, and saliva helps begin digestion.
The stomach mixes food; the small intestine absorbs many nutrients, while the large intestine absorbs water from the remains.
units.workedExample: Cooked maize is chewed in the mouth before moving down the oesophagus.
units.question: Where are many food nutrients absorbed?
units.feedback: The small intestine absorbs much of the digested food's nutrients.

exercises.question: Why does clean food matter?
exercises.answer: It lowers the risk of illness.

assignment.title: The digestive system — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw an original labelled digestive-system diagram and describe four organs.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: New learner diagram; PlusOne Grade 5 Teacher's Guide Unit 1 for topic reference.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Preventing water pollution
units.objective: Suggest ways to protect rivers and wells.
explanation: Water can be polluted by litter, sewage, chemicals and oils. Polluted water can damage aquatic habitats and cause illness.
Communities can dispose of waste properly, protect wells, maintain sanitation and report spills. Water that looks clean can still be unsafe.
units.workedExample: A school covers a well opening and keeps waste bins away from the water source.
units.question: Which action protects a river?
units.feedback: Preventing rubbish from entering water reduces pollution.

assignment.title: Preventing water pollution — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Create a safe map sketch of a local water source with two risks and proposed solutions.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Original map drawing; PlusOne Grade 5 Teacher's Guide Unit 3.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Using solar energy
units.objective: Describe uses and limits of solar power.
explanation: Sunlight provides energy that can help heat water or produce electricity through a solar panel. Solar lamps can support evening study.
Solar electricity generation is reduced at night and during heavy cloud cover. Safe battery storage can help manage the difference.
units.workedExample: A small solar panel charges a lamp during the day so it can be used in the evening.
units.question: Which changes sunlight into electricity?
units.feedback: Photovoltaic solar panels convert light into electricity.

assignment.title: Using solar energy — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Design a labelled poster of three community solar-energy uses and one limitation.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: New poster; PlusOne Grade 5 Teacher's Guide Unit 24.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Writing a short summary
units.objective: Retell main points in fewer words.
explanation: A summary tells readers the main ideas of a passage without repeating every sentence. Read first for meaning and then identify key details.
Remove repeated information, keep important facts in order and rewrite in your own words. Check that the summary still makes sense.
units.workedExample: Original: Children planted trees and watered them daily. Summary: Children cared for new trees.
units.question: What should a summary include?
units.feedback: A useful summary keeps the essential information.

exercises.question: What is a main idea?
exercises.answer: The central point of a text.

assignment.title: Writing a short summary — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Summarise a teacher-created environmental passage in 50–70 words.

units.mediaActivity: Original short passage written by school staff.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Whole numbers to one million
units.objective: Read, expand and compare large numbers.
explanation: A digit's place determines its value. In 742,506 the 7 means seven hundred thousand and 4 means forty thousand.
Compare numbers from the highest place value first. Expanded form separates a number into the total of its component place values.
units.question: What is 8 worth in 803,214?
units.feedback: The 8 occupies the hundred-thousands place.

exercises.question: Is 29 prime?
exercises.answer: Yes. Its only factors are 1 and 29.

assignment.title: Whole numbers to one million — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Use a place-value chart to expand five six-digit numbers and explain the largest.

units.mediaActivity: Homemade place-value abacus; PlusOne Grade 6 Mathematics Revision Unit 1.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Adding proper fractions
units.objective: Use equivalent fractions when adding.
explanation: When fractions have the same denominator, add the numerators and keep the denominator. For example, 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7.
For unlike denominators, first change them to equal denominators. One half equals two quarters, so 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4.
units.workedExample: Two eighths plus three eighths equals five eighths: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8.
units.question: What is 2/7 + 3/7?
units.feedback: Two sevenths plus three sevenths makes five sevenths.

assignment.title: Adding proper fractions — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw two fraction strips and explain how they help solve three addition problems.

units.mediaActivity: Original folded-paper strips; PlusOne Grade 6 Mathematics Revision Unit 8.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Using ratios
units.objective: Compare quantities and produce equivalent ratios.
explanation: A ratio compares quantities, such as two mangoes to three oranges. It can be written 2:3.
Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number. For example, 2:3 is the same as 4:6.
units.workedExample: If a recipe uses 1 cup juice to 2 cups water, doubling gives 2 cups juice to 4 cups water.
units.question: Which ratio is equivalent to 3:4?
units.feedback: Multiplying both parts of 3:4 by two gives 6:8.

assignment.title: Using ratios — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Survey two classroom categories, give their ratio and show an equivalent ratio.

units.mediaActivity: Counters or teacher-made ratio chart; PlusOne Grade 6 Mathematics Revision Unit 12.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: A formal request letter
units.objective: Write a polite letter explaining a problem and solution.
explanation: A formal letter has a clear purpose, respectful greeting and organised body paragraphs. It is usually addressed to a person or office in an official capacity.
Explain what happened using reliable facts, describe why it matters, propose a practical action and close courteously.
units.workedExample: Subject: Request to repair the school tap. I kindly request repairs because learners need clean water.
units.question: Which sentence fits a formal letter?
choices: I request that the damaged tap be repaired.
units.feedback: A formal letter is respectful and specific.

exercises.question: Name a feature of formal tone.

assignment.title: A formal request letter — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Write a 150–200 word letter about an environmental improvement; avoid publishing personal addresses.

units.mediaActivity: Original layout; Grade 6 English learner's book formal-letter unit.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Reporting real observations
units.objective: Write an accurate short report using headings.
explanation: A report states what was observed and organises facts into sections. Include a clear title and a brief explanation of the activity.
Separate what you actually observed from opinions. Give recommendations based on the evidence rather than inventing measurements.
units.workedExample: Inspection: Three garden beds had seedlings and one needed watering. Recommendation: Water the dry bed.
units.question: What should a report contain?
units.feedback: Reports should state actual observations accurately.

assignment.title: Reporting real observations — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Observe a classroom space with a teacher, then write a dated report and two recommendations.

units.mediaActivity: Original checklist for school garden observations.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Planning balanced meals
units.objective: Identify food groups in locally available meals.
explanation: Different foods provide energy, protein, vitamins and minerals. A varied meal can combine a staple with beans, vegetables and clean drinking water.
Lack of important nutrients may cause deficiency problems. Food planning should consider safety, affordability and locally available foods.
units.workedExample: Sadza, beans and leafy vegetables supply a range of food components.
units.question: Which meal offers greater variety?
units.feedback: A varied meal includes different food groups.

exercises.question: Name two nutrient groups.
exercises.answer: Carbohydrates and proteins, or other suitable groups.

exercises.question: Why eat varied foods?
exercises.answer: Different nutrients support different body functions.

assignment.title: Planning balanced meals — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Plan a one-day menu and show food groups and approximate affordability.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Student-drawn balanced-meal plate; PlusOne Grade 6 Science Nutrition.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Water filtration and safe storage
units.objective: Explain limits of filtration and methods to save water.
explanation: Settling and filtration can remove some particles from muddy water. They do not by themselves guarantee removal of germs or harmful dissolved chemicals.
Proper treatment depends on the water source and public-health advice. Cover stored water, repair leaks and do not drink classroom model water.
units.workedExample: A sand-and-gravel model makes water less cloudy, but the result is marked NOT FOR DRINKING.
units.question: Does simple filtration guarantee safe drinking water?
units.feedback: Simple filtering may leave germs and chemicals.

exercises.question: Name a way to save water.

assignment.title: Water filtration and safe storage — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Build a supervised non-drinking filter model and write five safety precautions.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Original supervised model; PlusOne Grade 6 Science Water.

units.subject: Indigenous Languages
units.title: Proverbs about cooperation
units.objective: Explain how proverbs express community values.
explanation: Indigenous proverbs communicate ideas through short memorable sayings. Meanings may depend on the speaker's language and local situation.
The Shona saying 'Rume rimwe harikombi churu' can encourage cooperation. Invite equivalent proverbs in other Zimbabwean languages and discuss their context.
units.workedExample: A group completes a community task by sharing effort; a proverb can reinforce teamwork.
units.question: Which action shows cooperation?
units.feedback: Working together is a way of demonstrating community care.

exercises.question: Explain the proverb used.
exercises.answer: One person alone may struggle; cooperation helps.

exercises.question: Give a context for a proverb.

assignment.title: Proverbs about cooperation — class assignment
assignment.instructions: With permission, collect two proverbs and explain their lessons and where they are used.

units.mediaActivity: Consent-based oral interview; original illustrations only.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Breathing and the diaphragm
units.objective: Describe airflow and the diaphragm's role.
explanation: Air enters through the nose or mouth and passes down the trachea into the bronchi and lungs. Oxygen crosses from air sacs into the bloodstream.
The diaphragm contracts and moves down as we inhale, helping the lungs expand. Normal exhalation lets it relax and rise.
units.workedExample: During inhalation the diaphragm moves downward and the chest has more space for air.
units.question: Which tube carries air towards the lungs?
units.feedback: The trachea is the windpipe leading to the bronchi.

exercises.question: What does the diaphragm do on inhalation?

assignment.title: Breathing and the diaphragm — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw and label an original respiratory-system diagram and describe inhalation.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Learner-created diagram; PlusOne Grade 7 Science Unit 1.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Comparing energy sources
units.objective: Identify renewable and non-renewable resources.
explanation: Sunlight and wind are replenished naturally. Coal and petroleum form over geological time and are regarded as non-renewable fuels.
All energy choices have costs and limitations. Compare reliability, availability, emissions and safe handling when making recommendations.
units.workedExample: A solar panel supplies power in sunshine, while a diesel generator uses a fuel that produces emissions.
units.question: Which source is renewable?
units.feedback: Sunlight is continuously replenished.

exercises.question: Why conserve energy?
exercises.answer: To limit waste and environmental impacts.

assignment.title: Comparing energy sources — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Compare three energy sources used locally in a table of benefits and limitations.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Original energy comparison chart; PlusOne Grade 7 Science Energy.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Reduce, reuse and recycle
units.objective: Plan safe waste reduction in school.
explanation: Reduce means use less unnecessary material. Reuse means safely use an item again. Recycle means processing certain materials into something new.
Children should never sort sharp, medical or chemical waste. A class can examine clean paper, cardboard and safe containers with adult supervision.
units.workedExample: Use both sides of a sheet before placing suitable paper in a recycling collection.
units.question: What is an example of reuse?
choices: Using a clean jar for storage
units.feedback: A clean jar can be reused for another purpose.

exercises.question: What is recycling?
exercises.answer: Processing suitable waste into new products.

assignment.title: Reduce, reuse and recycle — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Complete a supervised count of safe classroom waste and suggest three reductions.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030
units.mediaActivity: Student-created waste audit chart; PlusOne Grade 7 Science Sustainable Resources.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Reading bar graphs
units.objective: Interpret frequencies and compare groups.
explanation: A bar graph shows category quantities with bars. Read the graph title and axis scale before comparing heights.
Subtract category totals to find differences and add them to find totals. Draw bars of equal width with a consistent scale.
units.workedExample: Garden survey: maize 12, beans 8, tomatoes 6. Total = 26 plants.
units.question: How many more maize than tomato plants?

exercises.question: What should the vertical axis show?

assignment.title: Reading bar graphs — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Survey a safe classroom topic, make a labelled bar graph and explain three observations.

units.mediaActivity: Original tally and bar chart.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Percentages and discounts
units.objective: Find percentages of quantities and final prices.
explanation: Percent means per hundred. Ten percent can be found by dividing by ten, and twenty-five percent is one quarter.
To work out a discount, calculate the saving first and subtract it from the starting price. State currency units clearly.
units.workedExample: A US$24 bag reduced by 25% saves US$6 and costs US$18.
units.question: What is 20% of 60?

assignment.title: Percentages and discounts — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Prepare three hypothetical prices for school items, apply a 10% discount and show all steps.

units.mediaActivity: Handwritten price cards; PlusOne Grade 6 Mathematics Revision Percentages background.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Persuasive writing for school improvement
units.objective: Support a claim using reasons and evidence.
explanation: A persuasive paragraph expresses a clear viewpoint. Explain why it matters using logical reasons, examples or reliable observations.
Link points using words such as 'because' and 'therefore'. Be respectful and avoid inventing data to strengthen an argument.
units.workedExample: Our school should repair leaking taps because water is essential and leaks waste resources.
units.question: Which sentence gives a clear reason?
choices: We should fix leaks because water is precious.
units.feedback: The sentence links a proposal with a clear reason.

exercises.question: Write one persuasive claim.
exercises.answer: Specific claim for a safe improvement.

assignment.title: Persuasive writing for school improvement — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Write 180–220 original words recommending a practical school improvement and give three supporting reasons.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Hearing and naming everyday sounds
units.objective: Identify two everyday sounds through listening and observation.
explanation: Different things make different sounds. A door may knock, a bird may sing and people may clap their hands when they are happy.
Listen to a trusted teacher make safe sounds. Say or sign the object you heard and describe whether it was loud, soft or repeated.
units.workedExample: A teacher claps once, then twice. The sounds come from the teacher's hands.
units.question: Which action makes a clapping sound?
units.feedback: Hands touching together make a clap.

exercises.question: Listen and identify a hand clap.

assignment.title: Hearing and naming everyday sounds — class assignment
assignment.instructions: With a teacher, identify three familiar sounds and draw one source.

units.mediaActivity: Original teacher-made sound activity; no commercial illustration.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Saying hello and goodbye
units.objective: Use greetings during arrival and departure.
explanation: Greeting someone is a way to begin a conversation politely. A learner can say 'Hello' to a friend and 'Good morning' at the start of a school day.
When leaving, say 'Goodbye'. Listen to the other person's response, and use signing or a familiar language when needed.
units.workedExample: Teacher: 'Good morning.' Child: 'Good morning, Teacher.'
units.question: Which word can we say when leaving?
units.feedback: Goodbye is a suitable farewell.

assignment.title: Saying hello and goodbye — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Act out meeting and leaving a friend with a teacher's support.

units.mediaActivity: Teacher-led greeting role-play.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: My body and clean hands
units.objective: Name basic body parts and practise clean habits.
explanation: We use our hands to hold objects and our feet to walk. Our eyes help us see and our ears help us hear different sounds.
Keeping clean is important. A teacher can demonstrate washing hands with soap and clean water after play and before eating.
units.workedExample: A child touches the ears when asked 'Show your ears' and then names the hands used to clap.
units.question: Which body part helps us hear?
units.feedback: Ears help us hear sounds.

exercises.question: Name the body part used for walking.

assignment.title: My body and clean hands — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw a person and label or point to three body parts; demonstrate a handwashing step.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Infant Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Seeds, leaves and growing plants
units.objective: Recognise a plant and name simple parts.
explanation: Plants grow in many places including gardens and school grounds. Some grow from seeds into young plants with stems and leaves.
We can look at a plant without pulling it from the ground. Under supervision, show its leaves and stem and describe what it needs to grow.
units.workedExample: A bean seed placed in suitable soil and watered may grow a small shoot.
units.question: Which part of a plant is often green and flat?
units.feedback: Leaves are often green and flat.

exercises.question: Name something plants need.
exercises.answer: Water, light or suitable growing medium.

exercises.question: What can grow into a new plant?

assignment.title: Seeds, leaves and growing plants — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Observe a safe plant in the school yard, draw it and point to its leaves.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Infant Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030

units.subject: Indigenous Languages
units.title: Listening to local rhymes
units.objective: Listen to and join a short familiar rhyme.
explanation: Rhymes and songs help children practise listening and speaking. Families and communities have different locally meaningful rhymes.
Listen carefully to a short rhyme taught by a teacher. Repeat or sign a phrase and clap along to its rhythm while respecting other learners' language choices.
units.workedExample: A teacher says a simple original greeting rhyme and learners repeat the last line together.
units.question: What should you do first when learning a rhyme?
units.feedback: Listening helps us follow a rhyme's rhythm and words.

exercises.question: Show rhythm in a safe way.

assignment.title: Listening to local rhymes — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Share a short community-approved rhyme or greeting and explain when it is used.

units.mediaActivity: Use teacher-authored or community-permitted recordings only.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Recognising beginning sounds
units.objective: Connect simple spoken sounds with beginning letters.
explanation: Words have sounds that we can hear. The word 'mat' begins with the /m/ sound while 'sun' begins with /s/.
Say a word slowly and listen for its first sound. Use picture cards that the teacher has drawn, rather than guessing from spelling alone.
units.workedExample: The word 'ball' begins with the /b/ sound.
units.question: What sound begins 'sun'?
units.feedback: The first sound in sun is /s/.

exercises.question: Name a word beginning /m/.
exercises.answer: Mat, man or another correct word.

assignment.title: Recognising beginning sounds — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Draw four objects and match each to the first letter of its name.

units.mediaActivity: Original picture phonics cards.

units.subject: English Language
units.title: Writing sentences from pictures
units.objective: Use capital letters and full stops in short sentences.
explanation: A sentence tells a complete idea. Start with a capital letter and use a full stop at the end of a statement.
Look at a picture or real scene. Say what is happening, then write the idea in a clear sentence that the reader can understand.
units.workedExample: The child waters the plants. This sentence starts with a capital and ends with a full stop.
units.question: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
units.feedback: The second sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

exercises.question: Write a sentence about a tree.

assignment.title: Writing sentences from pictures — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Write five short sentences describing original drawings or things seen at school.

units.mediaActivity: Teacher-created picture prompts.

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Caring for teeth
units.objective: Name types of teeth and ways to maintain dental hygiene.
explanation: Teeth help us bite and chew food. Different teeth have different shapes; some cut food while others grind it.
Brushing with appropriate toothpaste, keeping toothbrushes clean and visiting a dental professional when possible help protect oral health.
units.workedExample: Molars have broad chewing surfaces useful for grinding food.
units.question: Which teeth mainly grind food?
units.feedback: Molars have broad surfaces used in grinding.

assignment.title: Caring for teeth — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Prepare a tooth-care poster showing safe hygiene routines and name two types of teeth.

units.syllabusSource: MoPSE Junior Science and Technology Syllabus 2024–2030

units.subject: Science and Technology
units.title: Safe food handling
units.objective: Explain ways to prevent food contamination.
explanation: Food may become unsafe when harmful germs or dirt enter it. Wash hands and clean preparation surfaces before handling food.
Keep raw and ready-to-eat foods separate where appropriate, cover food, and use safe storage conditions. Ask a responsible adult when unsure.
units.workedExample: A child washes hands and uses a clean plate before serving fruit.
units.question: Which habit helps protect food?
units.feedback: Clean utensils help reduce contamination.

exercises.question: Name two hygiene practices.
exercises.answer: Wash hands, clean surfaces or cover food.

exercises.question: Who should supervise heat or knives?

assignment.title: Safe food handling — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Create a four-step illustrated guide to safely preparing a simple snack.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Finding fractions of quantities
units.objective: Work out unit fractions and related quantities.
explanation: A fraction represents equal parts of a whole. The denominator names how many equal parts there are, and the numerator names how many are chosen.
To find one-quarter of a number, divide by four. To find three quarters, multiply that answer by three.
units.workedExample: Three quarters of 20 = (20 ÷ 4) × 3 = 15.
units.question: What is 3/4 of 12?
units.feedback: A quarter of 12 is 3, so three quarters is 9.

assignment.title: Finding fractions of quantities — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Use bottle tops to demonstrate three fractions of quantities and explain the calculations.

units.mediaActivity: Original fraction counters.

units.subject: Indigenous Languages
units.title: Summarising a community story
units.objective: Identify a story's main idea and lesson in a familiar language.
explanation: Stories told in an indigenous language preserve family experiences and cultural knowledge. Listen or read carefully before summarising.
Select the main events and the message, but leave out details that are not essential. The teacher may invite translations where learners use different home languages.
units.workedExample: A story about neighbours sharing seeds may be summarised as a lesson on cooperation and helping each other.
units.question: What belongs in a story summary?
units.feedback: A summary focuses on essential events and their meaning.

assignment.title: Summarising a community story — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Summarise a community-approved story in your home language and explain its value.

units.mediaActivity: Original locally permitted storytelling; respect storyteller ownership.

units.subject: Indigenous Languages
units.title: Writing about a traditional skill
units.objective: Write a structured account of a heritage skill with respectful explanation.
explanation: Heritage skills can include weaving, pottery, farming methods and music. A clear composition describes the skill, the tools and the order of key activities.

Use appropriate vocabulary in the indigenous language being studied. Describe where the information came from, respect the knowledge holder and do not claim to have witnessed activities that were only described.
units.workedExample: A learner explains that a woven basket is made by preparing safe plant fibres and interlacing them in a planned pattern.
units.question: What strengthens a heritage composition?
units.feedback: A well-organised account uses a clear sequence and accurate local information.

exercises.question: Name a heritage skill.
exercises.answer: Weaving, pottery, farming or suitable example.

exercises.question: What should a process description include?
Why acknowledge an informant?
exercises.answer: Respect for the source of knowledge.

assignment.title: Writing about a traditional skill — class assignment
assignment.instructions: Write an original composition about a local traditional skill, based on your observation or a consented interview.

units.mediaActivity: Learner's own drawing or authorised community media only.
